utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. All the accused are here. Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey. Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Ms. Nikolic. The witness is already present in the courtroom. Unless there are preliminaries, we can start straightaway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to continue with your testimony. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jevdjevic. Mr. Jevdjevic, before we continue where we left off yesterday, I wish to go back a day in the chronology of events, and could we have 5D1106, please. While we are waiting for this document to come up on the screen, I'd like to ask you the following: In principle, as a rule, are you aware in general terms whether the protected areas of Srebrenica and Zepa were passable for humanitarian convoys and whether they went through?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that those two protected areas, that humanitarian convoys went there, and they passed through our territory, our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you go back in your memory to the 4th of July, 1995, which was a time of preparation for the operation carried out in the direction of Srebrenica, and can you tell us whether on that day and in any case before the 5th of July you observed movements of the army of Republika Srpska, hasty movements, through the territory of the Drina Corps before the 5th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we left off -- Mr. Jevdjevic, are you aware, while we still have the document on the screen, that on the 4th of July convoys passed through the zone of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not have any precise information as to convoys passing through on the 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any doubts as regards this combat report dated the 4th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't had occasion to see this document before, which is why I've read it now. There document deals with the passage of UNPROFOR convoys at various check-points and border crossings. It describes the composition of those convoys. I have no doubts about this report, because everything I know from that period of time tells me that it was quite normal and routine for convoys to pass through in this manner and that there were never any major problems as regards the passage of convoys to the protected areas and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We will not be needing this document anymore. Yesterday, on page 29481 in line 16, you said that in the spring of 1993 the Drina Corps participated in offensive actions in Cerska and Konjevic Polje, inter alia, Srebrenica, Zeleni Jadar, Pribicevac. My question is as follows. After that, you spoke about the forces which were prepared to participate in the operation against Srebrenica in July 1995, and my question was the following: Can you draw a comparison as regards the equivalence of the forces participating in the combat operations around Srebrenica in 1993 and the number of forces participating in 1995 in June?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know personally - because I participated in both of those operations of the corps, both in the spring of 1993 and in July [as interpreted] 1995, in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps - is that they were much large and professional forces participating in 1993 compared to the ones planned for 1995, because in the spring of 1993 around Srebrenica we had, so to speak, the most elite units which were engaged in that area. I am referring particularly to the Guards Brigade, to the Protection Regiment units, the Podrinje detachment of special forces, and some MUP units, in addition to our other units, so that both as regards manpower and the elite character of the units, I am sure that in 1993 we had larger and more elite forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please slow down when answering, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I wish to correct the transcript on page 3 in line 16. Instead of June, it should say July 1995. Could we now have 5D1105.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said, I knew more or less what units were participating and what their main tasks and axes of attack were. Mr. Jevdjevic, did you know on the 5th of July when you set out what the ultimate goal of the action Krivaja 95 was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before I set out to carry out the corp task, Krivaja 95, until around the 10th of July, in my estimation, I had an idea, and that's how the task was convoyed to me orally when I set out to carry it out, that the goal of the operation was to reduce the Srebrenica enclave to the borders of the demilitarised zone and taking up those key features on the south and south-east in order to prevent any further communication between those two enclaves and incursions of combat units from those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 2 here of this order -- or, rather, if you look at the preamble, does what you know correspond to what the corps commander Milenko Zivanovic is saying here?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that Drina Corps units have the task of separating the enclaves and to confine the Srebrenica enclave to an area which the international community calls the demilitarised or safe areas. It's not really very legible. It was sent on the 5th of July, and that was what I knew when I set out to carry out this task in the Pribicevac area on the 5th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please look at item 1, bullet point 3, and tell us whether the task given to the 1st and the 5th Podrinje Brigades also implies a simultaneous attack on Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that these two brigades, the 1st and the Podrinje Infantry Brigades, have the task of tying down the enemy forces as far as possible and in this way coordinate with the forces acting in the direction of the Srebrenica enclave. So their task was to engage in demonstrative activity in a show of force in order to create an impression in the Zepa Brigade that certain combat actions are being carried out in order to trick them, to mislead them and prevent them from coming to the assistance of the forces of the 28th Brigade in Srebrenica. So this was simply a show of force on the part of those two brigades of the Drina Corps, because each of them had only one battalion holding the front line towards the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also said that at the Pribicevac forward command post, you arrived there in the early afternoon on the 5th of July. Can you tell us which officers of the Drina Corps were at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that on the 5th of July Colonel Vicic arrived -he was the operations man in the Drina Corps - and some of the non-commissioned officers from the Staff Command who had logistical duties, and I think that in the early morning hours on the following day General Krstic arrived at the forward command post. He was the chief of staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were there any other officers from the Drina Corps who arrived there on the 5th or 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any other officers from the Drina Corps, except there may have been some subordinate commanders of various units who were deploying their units and preparing for the operation. At the forward command post, Colonel Vukota was there from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know the intelligence man of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period just before this operation, I don't know how long before, the assistant commander for intelligence was Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric, and I think he arrived at the forward command post in Pribicevac together with General Krstic in the early morning of the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We have had occasion here -- I won't go into this in great detail, but just for the record, we have heard about the existence of the so-called mobile com centre, this communications centre that you set up at this forward command post. Was it mobile?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a mobile communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, Mr. Jevdjevic, when did combat activity against Srebrenica begin?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat activities as part of the Krivaja 95 operation began in the early morning of the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did combat continue only during the daylight hours?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat actions were carried out only during daylight, when there was visibility, from the early morning until nightfall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of July, did anyone from the Main Staff come to the forward command post of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the axis of attack towards Srebrenica was -- from what direction it came?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Zeleni Jadar along the Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica road. That is Zeleni Jadar, Javor, Tucak, that was the axis along the Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica road, and the other axis of attack was from the general area of the village of Podravanije, Mount Klokoc, Caurka, Kostur. Those were mountain tops -- a cluster of mountain tops in the direction of Alibegovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And do you know from the north, to the north of the enclave, what unit of the Drina Corps held its positions there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the north, that was the Rudnik, Gunjaci, Bracan sectors. Positions were held by the Milici Infantry Brigade, and to the east from Kuarac to Zenika, that was the Zvornik Brigade [as interpreted]. I think -- I know that they had their tasks, but I know that those tasks had more to do with the show of force and efforts to tie down the enemy on that part of the front line because those units did not have rapid reaction or manoeuvre units, units that would be capable of engaging in purely offensive actions in attacks. So those were more show-of-force-type actions in that part of the front line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just received a suggestion that there is an error in the transcript at page 7, line 14. Instead of "Zvornik Brigade," it should read "Bratunac Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, did you indeed say that this was the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Bratunac Brigade. It had its positions to the east, and it engaged in show-of-force actions in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And this does not -- this did not include any efforts to advance in the direction of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in fact until the 11th, which was the day when the -- this area was captured militarily, that they did not move from their initial positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, could you please tell us, on the 7th of July, did combat continue in the direction of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that on the second day of the operation, that was the 7th of July, it rained in the night between the 6th and the 7th of July, and the day was foggy and wet, and the visibility on the front line was very bad, and the Drina Corps units in that area were settling down, arranging its combat dispositions, but there was no combat on that day, no fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we just get one foundational question? How does he know all this? Is he getting reports? Is he listening to the radio? I mean, he's the coms guy. Why does he know all this if he is in his coms vehicle or what? Just -- I'm sure he can answer it quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Fair enough. Could you clarify this for us, Mr. Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I stayed with the communications equipment at all times, in the key moments of the operation, and all the communications that were going on between the commander of the operation - that was General Krstic - and his subordinate commanders literally went through my ears because this equipment had a loudspeaker, and all the communication between the brigades and the brigade commanders and the corps commander was audible through this loudspeaker just as we can now hear each other here in this courtroom, and that was how I was able to monitor, to follow what was going on on the front line at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you say a brigade, do you mean units that took part in those combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean. The selected units, those were combat groups that the brigade set up from their original formation and dispatched them to participate in this Operation Krivaja 95. So when I say the brigade, I am referring to those groups from the original brigades that took part in Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you have an encrypted communications network with those units?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the commanders of those units, the combat groups that took part in this operation, we did have an encrypted radio network that we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could we please have 4D327. Mr. Jevdjevic, could you please look at item 2, "Combat readiness" -- "State Of Combat Readiness," and this part that begins with the word "The units..." That would be the second or third passage. Could you please read it to yourself, and then I'll be asking you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This description of the situation in this regular combat report, does this correspond to what was actually going on on the 8th of July in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that our units carried out the first initial combat operations on the 8th of July, and it is indicated here that an advance of one kilometre was achieved, and this probably also counts the area, the no man's land between the two units, except for this part where it says part of the units and the Ministry of the Interior forces are constantly patrolling the territory -- or are constantly controlling the territory. I was not aware of it at the time, and this report was probably drafted at the Drina Corps command at Vlasenica, and they probably knew that, but as far as I was concerned, I knew the first thing about the front line. I was aware of the situation at the front line in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next document is 6D22. Could we please scroll down this document in the Serbian version so that we could see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, this is a document. It's a report from the forward command post at Pribicevac. First of all, I would like to ask you because you're an expert, you see that there is a handwritten note at the bottom of the document in Roman alphabet. It says: "Received on the 9th of July, 1995, at 2320." BR number, 36. It is unclear whether it is indeed 36 or maybe some corrections were made here, and there's a signature. Can you explain to us, what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you can all see that this is 1995. I thought that you had said 1955. The handwritten note was written by my encryptions officer. He was with me at Pribicevac at the forward command post, and he sent this interim combat report from the forward command post at Pribicevac to the Drina Corps command, and he noted down here, since for the special kind of mobile communications centre we did not have the stamp that is ordinarily used, he simply jotted down that this telegram was received successfully by the communications centre in Vlasenica, the Drina Corps command, at 2320 hours on the 9th of July. This is his signature, and this is the number of the telegram itself. I don't know whether it's 36 or maybe some other number, but that's rather immaterial.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And in accordance with your rules, when handwritten notes of this kind are made by the encryption officer, should he also indicate where the -- when the telegram was sent and when the telegram was received by the unit to whom it was addressed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can easily rephrase it, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, do you know what the encryption officer that is actually sending the telegram must write down?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an internal rule among the encryption officers. I knew about it, although I'm not an encryption officer myself. In order to be certain that the other side received the telegram, because the communications equipment that we used could be jammed at times, and it is sufficient for the telegram -- it takes four or five minutes to send a telegram or even maybe more. It is sufficient for just a tiny little disruption to occur in the electromagnetic area and the whole telegram cannot be sent. This happened often with the forward command posts. .I don't know whether it was because of the jamming on the part of the enemy, but we had to resend telegrams often. That is why the encryption officers had to write down the time when the other side received the telegram, that is, when his opposite number in the Drina Corps command confirmed the receipt of this telegram. It is easy to check this. For instance, if there is a document at the Drina Corps command where this telegram was received, the same time should be indicated there, 2320, because the encryption officer writes down the time when a receipt is confirmed by his opposite number, and that is why it is indicated here, received at such-and-such time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And this note, at any rate, is made at the Pribicevac forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is very much leading, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the question, and I'm happy with the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to ask you to repeat it because I wasn't quite sure I heard it -- I heard, but if you are withdrawing the question, I think you have to remain very unhappy with the answer, which will no longer be in the record. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, where was this note made?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was made at the forward command post at Pribicevac, and I indicated at the beginning of my answer that this was written down by my encryption officer at Pribicevac. That's what I said right at the beginning of my first answer, and you can check that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, let us go back to the topic of the combat operations that were ongoing. We are now on the 9th of July. Do you know that in that area, the area where combat operations were going on, that the Dutch Battalion of the peacekeeping force was present?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with them in the course of the combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was in contact with them only once. It was on the 9th. I think those were the UNPROFOR members who were at the observation post in the Zeleni Jadar sector. Now I'm speaking about myself. And through the communications network, I heard the commanders carrying out attacks on their designated axes report about UNPROFOR, about encountering observation posts on their attack axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And what was this personal contact that you had with UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th of July, on the axis of attack of our forces, that was Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica, there was an incident at the observation post. I heard about it at the communications centre. One of the commanders carrying out an attack on this axis reported to General Krstic that the forces of the 28th Division opened fire on them and that a soldier was killed in this fire, and -- and that they started pulling out towards our forces and went towards Zeleni Jadar behind our lines. And since I was the only officer close to General Krstic, he was there by the radio, in an effort to solve -- solve this unpleasant situation - unpleasant for UNPROFOR, that is - he ordered me as a professional officer to go down there to Zeleni Jadar as soon as possible and to receive the UNPROFOR soldiers from the observation post and to take them to safe -- to a safe area, in other words, to Pribicevac. That's what I did. I went down to Zeleni Jadar, and I encountered them. They were in four armoured personnel carriers. They were already moving from Zeleni Jadar to the roads leading to Pribicevac, and I turned my vehicle around, and I led them to the safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you disarm them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think there are reports to that effect. They were in their combat vehicles. They did not leave their combat vehicles at all. The gunner was on the turret manning the machine-gun. They went to Pribicevac, remained there for a while, and then I suppose on the orders of their superior command, they headed to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, at that time did you have or did any orders reach you as to how the units participating in combat should treat the civilian population? We saw how they treated UNPROFOR. Were you able to hear anything through the communications network as to how they should treat the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard General Krstic telling his commanders quite simply that they should avoid any kind of conflict with UNPROFOR or any kind of fire on UNPROFOR, that they should avoid any sort of firing on civilians. We had no information that there actually were any civilians in the combat area, and I think that in that period some telegrams with similar contents arrived from the superior commands as regards the civilian population, property, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P33, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, please take a look at this last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When referring to the telegrams arriving from the superior command concerning the treatment of civilians, are you referring to this telegram?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the telegram, but I think there was another one that arrived in the afternoon of the 11th. The reason I remember it is that there was no one from the command at the forward command post at the time, so I read the telegram. But I'm also referring to this one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have document 5D1375, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, do you know who Dragomir Vasic is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Dragomir Vasic. Not especially well, but I do know that he was the chief of the public security station in Zvornik and that he remained at that post after the war. I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We're still dealing with the 9th of July, and it's quite clear from this that someone signed this telegram on behalf of Mr. Vasic. However, that's not all that important at present. And in this telegram, it says that in Srebrenica no population has been observed. That's what it says in the first paragraph of this dispatch, if we can call it that. Did your intelligence man give you any information as to where the civilian population was on the 9th of July, the population of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the forward command post there was the assistant for intelligence, and he had a vehicle at the forward command post with a small surveillance equipment, and we received daily information from him about the communications of the 28th Division and their intentions, and I did not have any information that on the 9th there were no inhabitants in Srebrenica. It seems quite illogical because of some events I experienced later on, the 10th and the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Well, of course we cannot establish from this telegram what time of day it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, although it says up there that it should be encrypted, but probably the cryptographer did not enter this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let's go to the sentence before the last in this telegram where it says: "There is information that the enemy is in disarray and is asking NATO to bomb." Did your surveillance centre have this information?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, no. On the 10th, we had quite reliable information after restoring certain trig points to the effect that enemy resistance was decreasing, but we didn't have this information on the 9th because combat was still underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Between you at the forward command post and the Zvornik security centre, was there any exchange of information on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 5D1365.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We're still on the 9th of July. It says in this document, in the first sentence: "The aggressor army entered the town at 1100 [as interpreted] hours from the direction of Zeleni Jadar (Ucina Basca). Our military command is dissolving and the members of the 28th Division of the ground forces..." and so on and so forth. Then it says that: "An urgent meeting is requested with the Serbian aggressors in order to find a possibility to open a corridor for the population to move out and to move to the nearest free territory of the Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina." Mr. Jevdjevic, did the forward command post receive this information?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we just -- I'm sorry, there was a -- it said 1100 hours. I think the document said 1800. It's probably an important time to get straight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will imagine you agree to that, Mr. Petrusic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 4D336, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, you had occasion to see this document. Can you tell us briefly what was happening on the 10th of July as regards the combat activities of the warring sides?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of July in the early morning, it was still dark, there was real panic at our forward command post because the enemy forces of the 28th Division from Srebrenica mounted a fierce counter-attack against a crucial facility or a crucial feature that we had taken in the course of that operation, which is Zivkovo Brdo. That's a hill several kilometres away from Srebrenica. We took it on the 9th. In the early morning hours, in that counter-attack by the 28th Division, our units were pushed back from that hill, and as it was still dark, the situation was unclear and very unfavourable for the forces of the Drina Corps. I think we had at least four or six men killed in that counter-attack by the 28th Division, and the front line stabilised only at around 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning when we were pushed back from that feature, Zivkovo Brdo hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did the units of the Drina Corps manage to come back to that feature in the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that 10th day, certain preparations were made. There was reorganisation. Some units were re-introduced which were able to conduct offensive action. At around noon on the 10th, the elevation of Zivkovo Brdo was retaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is that when combat ceased?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Combat continued, but it was my general impression that after our counter-attack and our retaking of Zivkovo Brdo, the resistance of the forces of the 28th Division was less and less well organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, did any officers from the Main Staff arrive at the forward command post in Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of July in the morning, I think it was around 9.00, the commander of the Main Staff General Mladic arrived at the forward command post. He was accompanied by General Zivanovic, who was the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long they stayed at the forward command post and what they did there, both of them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They remained at the forward command post, more specifically at a point -- an observation post 300 or 400 metres away from the forward command post, and they stayed there the whole day. I was able to follow through the radio communications that General Mladic, from the time of his arrival onwards, spoke on the network of command and control with our units participating in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know specifically to whom he issued orders?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know specifically because I remember very well the orders he issued to Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic when he spoke with him about the Zivkovo Brdo elevation. I also remember that he spoke to Colonel Andric at the time, who was attacking from the eastern side, from the direction of Podravanije, and that he personally issued certain orders to him when he reported to him about a line he had reached and his intention of taking a certain feature, and General Mladic had some assessments of his own that there were no enemy on those features and that they would be wasting time trying to take them. Instead, he urged him to go around that feature and continue the attack without getting his men tired needlessly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And what did continuing the attack imply?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Continuing the attack on the 10th, to the best of my knowledge, meant that this group of combat groups on the Srebrenica territory had the task of entering the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jevdjevic, on the 10th of July, as far as I can understand you, you did not enter the town.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 10th --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, where did your units remain in the course of the evening of the 19th -- or, rather, the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic himself was urging the commanders to take the dominant hills, which would enable them to exploit the success of their operations, and our units remained more or less -- I know that it was in the area of the Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica road near the villages of Vrajina and Bojna. Colonel Andric with his unit spent the night between the 10th and 11th in the village of Petrovici, which is below the Vagan hill, so those were the key units in the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us on the 11th of July how combat operations proceeded -- or, rather, what knowledge do you have, direct knowledge or knowledge that you gained from the radio traffic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the attack continued along the main axis and that our units reached the village of Bojna and that the remaining units were regrouping. Now I'm talking about the units that were attacking from the east. It was a company from the 2nd Romanija Brigade, and then at around noon or perhaps 13 or 1400 hours, the positions of our forces were attacked by NATO aircraft and Kuarac and Pribicevac sectors were also strafed by machine-guns from those aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And on the 10th -- or, rather, the 11th of July, did you know anything about the Milici Brigade, whether it was moving from its positions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the Milici Brigade, to the best of my recollection, throughout the operation up until the 11th it remained on its initial positions and was engaged in mainly show-of-force-type activities in order to tie down the enemy forces on that part of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After the NATO air-strikes on your positions, did General Mladic go back to the forward command post, and Generals Krstic, Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, do you know where after the air-strikes Generals Mladic, Krstic, and Zivanovic were?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the air-strikes, they were successively at two observations posts at Kula and Kuarac. Those are two hills near the Pribicevac forward command post, and to the best of my recollection, around one hour after the air-strikes ended and after the attack by our forces continued, they went in -- each in their own vehicle towards Srebrenica from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you remain at Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained at the Pribicevac forward command post, and I followed the developments, the combat situation, from radio traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the situation developed and how long you remained at Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that the forces of the 28th Division ceased with their resistance and that they pulled out from Srebrenica, for the most part to the broader -- in fact, to north-west, and that they were instructing the population from Srebrenica to go to the UNPROFOR compound at Potocari. The units that carried out the attack were setting up the combat disposition at the fringe areas, and I remained at the forward command post at Pribicevac up until around 1900 hours on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the troops, the soldiers, actually entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the mobile communications centre that was mounted on a vehicle, I and my soldiers went through Srebrenica on the 10th [as interpreted]. It was around -- at around 2000 hours. In the town itself, I did not see any of our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think there's just a mistake, in the English, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic. Do you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. It should say the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jevdjevic, you passed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed. Let's -- let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think Mr. Jevdjevic himself can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please just tell me what this is all about? Perhaps I made a slip of the tongue. It was the 11th, the 11th that I passed through Srebrenica. I can't recall what it was that I actually said, but the date is the 11th. That's when I left the forward command post. It was at around 2000 hours. Well, I stated this enumerable times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we want to hear. It's probably not your fault, anyway. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As you passed through Srebrenica, did you notice any damage in the town itself? I mean recent damage.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first time that I passed through the town ever, and I really paid attention as I was passing through this small town. I could see that there was damage caused by rifle bullets, holes on the facades of the houses. I don't know whether this was caused at an earlier date or when it was caused, but the town itself was rather dirty, and it was not well-kept. But I did not see a lot of damage caused by artillery pieces of a larger calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you notice any -- anything burning?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town itself I did not see anyone, and I couldn't see anyone who would be there to set things on fire. I saw just a few elderly people leaving Srebrenica in the direction of Potocari with -- with their luggage, and these are the only people that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you pass through Potocari on the 11th of July on your way to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At dusk I headed towards Bratunac taking the shortest route, and I passed through Potocari. It's a suburb around four kilometres away from Srebrenica, and I passed through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, did you notice anything in particular at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Potocari, I saw to the left and to the right of the road a huge number of civilians. I wouldn't want to make any estimates, but this is what I took away as an impression, a large number of civilians. I also saw UNPROFOR members. They were mingled in small groups. I could see the compound, which was to the right. I even saw the place where two or three armoured personnel carriers were fenced off. I assumed that this was a tank that had been seized, and I saw a few Serb soldiers with rifles on their soldiers talking to the civilians in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any instances of abuse or mistreatment of the civilians that you saw in Potocari done by the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I passed through Potocari, I did not stop my vehicle at all. I rolled past by the people very slowly because there were people on the road, too, and I did not observe any abuse or mistreatment or anything similar to that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And where did you go from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the command of the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac, passing through a check-point at the place called Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And whom did you find in the Bratunac Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got there, I first sought my communications officers -- officer who had gone with General Krstic to learn whether there were any news that affected me that had come in the meantime after I left for the Pribicevac forward command post. I also met with General Krstic, and later on, on the -- at 2200 hours on the 11th of July, I attended a meeting at the Bratunac Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, I will not examine you about this meeting. Could you just tell me briefly whether you left the forward command post at Pribicevac on your own initiative, or did somebody order you to -- did somebody order you to do so?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ordered me to pack up the communications centre and to leave the forward command post. It was my personal assessment. It was my own initiative, and soldiers are allowed to take it if they are ready to face the consequences, but we simply had information that the 28th Division is trying to break through in groups. Smaller elements were moving towards Zepa and some other areas, and a larger element was moving -- trying to move towards Tuzla, and I realised it would be dangerous to remain in that area, in that spot. And it is a matter of military logic that when the combat disposition moves, the forward command post must move with it. And I thought that I could establish a communications on the move if General Krstic needed it. So without any special orders on his part, I went to Bratunac, and he considered this to be quite normal and proper when we met in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Throughout this time, from the afternoon of the 11th when you parted ways with General Krstic, was General Krstic able to establish contact with you at all times?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My communications officer, my signals officer went with him. He had the encryption-enabled mobile communications equipment, and even if because of the lay of the land he was unable to establish contact with me, he could always establish contact with other participants in the command communications network, and then they could relay the message to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At this meeting at the Bratunac Brigade command, did you get any tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that meeting, General Mladic personally gave me a task, to set up the communications centre in Krivace that very evening, and that would be the communications centre for the attack on Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you in fact go to Krivace after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading. "Where did you go?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, after this meeting, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to carry out the task that I was given by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us what route you took?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bratunac, Kravica, Konjevic Polje, Kasaba, Milici, and up to Vlasenica where the corps command was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And en route, did you see any military units?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you notice any armed formations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the part of the road between Konjevic Polje and Kravica or somewhere there, I did notice two or three -- three smaller groups at various locations, groups of people wearing blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Blue uniforms were worn by MUP members, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object and ask that question be withdrawn and asked again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Do you wish to respond to that, Mr. Petrusic, before we decide?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you rephrase it, just give us a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you mind if I contributed to this, since this is my witness? There can't possibly be a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is it sensibly in dispute that MUP members wore blue uniforms or that this witness, who has given evidence for many, many days previously and been cross-examined by the Prosecution, went to Krivace after he left the meeting at Bratunac? These are all matters of adjudicated fact that are beyond context to quote back at Mr. McCloskey his own objections of yesterday. He really is just wasting the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is in contest about blue uniforms. We have seen lots of video and maybe one blue uniform. I don't want to get into the facts, but this is major area of contest. There is no evidence that there's anybody in blue uniforms and no significant evidence that I recall, anyway. So there's more to come before he comes to Krivace. So I've been trying not to object all the time, but I'm trying to object to get the time the message across that I prefer not to have leading so that when we get to the key areas the witness can answer. That's why I'm objecting at all. Some of these -- I will agree. Perhaps I don't need to object, but I'm trying to get the message across, which is not coming across. So now I'm going to be objecting all the time, which I prefer not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's make ourselves clear on this. In this Tribunal, in this Trial Chamber, we have always acknowledged the fact that leading questions can be made unless objected to. It doesn't mean to say that if they are objected to, and even if they are leading, it's always the case of disallowing them, particularly since although we adopt this common law approach in relation to leading questions. Still, this is a court of law where we don't have a jury, and the whole -- I mean, the main, main raison d'etre behind disallowing leading questions is perhaps the fact that there is a jury that can be unduly impressed. Now, we believe that we should be a little bit more tolerant in areas where we can safely proceed ahead without major confrontation or without major prejudice being caused. We don't feel that in this area, for example, the fact that the question was leading, and there is no doubt that it was leading, and is a major prejudice or any prejudice for that matter is being done, so we are allowing the question and suggest that we try to limit our objections as much as possible to when the case warrants an objection. Mr. Petrusic, do you want me to repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrusic's question was the following to you, Mr. Jevdjevic: He put it to you that blue uniforms were worn by MUP members, and he asks a rhetorical question whether this wasn't the case, and you had answered yes. Do you wish to add anything to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add to this except for the fact that I have no knowledge as to what unit, according to the establishment, those men belonged to, but I would see soldiers around every day, and yet on that day I saw men in blue uniforms, and I assumed that they were members of the civilian police. But as to what unit according to the establishment they belonged to, I don't know that to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we have the break now? If it's more convenient for you to finish this area, perhaps in the next two minutes or so, then we continue. Otherwise, we have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, you finally arrived in Vlasenica. Did you arrive there that night on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived in the command of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica at about 2400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this might be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have, incidentally, a 20-minute break today. The next break or the one following would also be of the same duration. However, we'll finish at quarter to 7.00 instead of at 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, in the course of yesterday you testified about the events connected with Zeleni Jadar in early June 1995 and said, inter alia, that you were among the participants in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have 5D1374, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This document is dated the 12th of June, 1995. It was issued by the Ministry of the Interior in Zvornik -- or, rather, its chief, the chief of the centre, Dragomir Vasic, and his signature is on the second page of this document. The document bears the title: "Information about the condition of the factory in Zeleni Jadar." Could we move to page 2, please. In the Serbian version, it's page 2, and also in the English version, also page 2, item 4 where it says the following: "The army has failed to do what has been agreed with President Karadzic because it has not seized another two elevations; in addition, the road leading to the factory is under the control of the Turks so that the equipment cannot be relocated." Mr. Jevdjevic, do you know something about an agreement between the army and President Karadzic concerning this action?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will no longer be needing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, I would like to move on to another topic. This will be my last topic, and it concerns the combat activities connected with Zepa. You told us that General Mladic, on the 11th of July in the evening, issued an order to you to establish a communications centre at Krivace. When did you set up this communications centre?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the new forward command post at Krivace, I established this new communications centre in the afternoon of the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P114, please. And we could go on to page 4 right away, item 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, did you or your communications organ participate in preparing the communications at the forward command post according to this item?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here the order is issued that in the village of Krivace, on the 13th of July at 1800 hours, the forward command post should begin functioning, and I had already set up the communications as an element of that forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And when you went to Zepa or at a later date, did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have P3748, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, this document -- well, is it familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen it. I saw it a few days ago when preparing for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know the code-name of operation -- or, rather, the operation that was connected with Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name was Stupcanica 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Here we see -- well, first of all, do you know who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the usher could show it to me. I assume it was the chief of communications of the corps, but if I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This document was drawn up and sent to these units by Lieutenant Colonel Nedo Blagojevic as it says on the telegram. He was the head of -- or chief of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, can you explain why on the 13th of July, 1995, when this communications plan was being forwarded, is the reference made to Operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably for the sole reason that the plan remained the same, the plan that had been used in Krivaja 95. So most probably the same plan was applied to the future operation. This telegram was sent only to two units which did not participate in Krivaja 95, and according to plan they were to take part in Stupcanica 95, and this was forwarded to them so that they would have the plan of the radio network.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, I don't want to delve into these communications further. I think we've heard enough about the communications systems in the army of Republika Srpska, but please tell us briefly whether this forward command post at Krivace functioned in the same way as regards communications as did the forward command post at Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in exactly the same way. The only thing that chained were the azimuths of the antennae in two locations, because the forward command post had moved to another location and two brigades were added on as reserve participants, two brigades which had not participated in the previous operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what officers of the Drina Corps were present at this forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Krivace forward command post and later on at other forward command post in Operation Stupcanica 95, the officers from the Drina Corps who were present were General Krstic; Colonel Vicic, an operations officer; Lieutenant Colonel Osoric, who was an intelligence man; and I think a staff sergeant from the corps command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his name, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name, please? Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, you mentioned General Krstic; Colonel Vicic, an operations officer. Can you tell us, who else was there among the officers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric and -- well, that was Svetozar Kosoric and Momir Amovic a staff sergeant from the Staff Command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you still at the communications lines as you had been during Operation Krivaja?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 5D1112, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, tell us briefly, when did the combat activities against Zepa begin?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And were they conducted continuously, without interruption?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, there were two or three cease-fires which lasted for different periods of time, and they had to do with the negotiations conducted by the two warring sides. The political and military authorities from Srebrenica negotiated with our negotiators concerning the hand-over of weapons and the evacuation of the population from Zepa. There were cease-fires during those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We have an interim combat report here, which is dated the 19th of July, 1995, and it refers to the cease-fire and the evacuation of Muslims from Zepa. Can you tell us, who participated on the side of the army of Republika Srpska? Who participated in these negotiations? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that but not directly, from my own experience. I know that the place where the negotiations were held was at Boksanica, near the observation post there, and I know through the communications that General Krstic took part. Well, I know that anyway. But I also know through the communications that from the military, from the army of Republika Srpska, it was General Mladic who participated in those negotiations. I assume that General Tolimir also took part in the negotiations, because according to the information that I received from the radio communications, he was at Boksanica, the sector of Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the presence of the representatives of the international community at those talks or negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic told me upon his return from one round of talks that the international community -- or, rather, the UNPROFOR was represented by General Smith. He was there with some of his officers, staff officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5D1116.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The date is the 25th of July. Mr. Jevdjevic, please tell me, at the time when you arrived at Zepa, at Krivace, some ten days had gone in the intervening period. Could you tell us who, if indeed anyone, from the Main Staff came to this forward command post where you were?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Krivace forward command post and later on at Glodjane, General Mladic came several times on behalf of the Main Staff or from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You told us that you did know about the participation of the members of the army of Republika Srpska and UNPROFOR in negotiations, and do you know who took part in the negotiations from the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked General Krstic upon his return from the negotiations on one occasion who participated from the opposite side, and he said that those were the representatives of the civilian authorities, Dr. Benjamin Kulovac and another man. I think his last name may have been Stitkovac or something like that, or Torlak, Hamdija Torlak, something to that effect. They were representatives of the political authorities in -- of the political government in Zepa, in the enclave of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document dated the 25th of July, 1995, and could you tell me, do you know that there was an evacuation of the civilian population from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long this evacuation lasted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you know or do you know whether representatives of UNPROFOR were present during the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And do you know what battalion or, rather, what military formation of the UN was deployed on observation posts in the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Ukrainian unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that this evacuation lasted for two days. Do you know how long the fighting around the enclave of Zepa lasted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the beginning of August. I think the 2nd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us if there was any resistance on the part of the Muslim armed units, and where did they mount this resistance after the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were negotiations going on about the evacuation of, first, the wounded and then the civilians and then the soldiers of Zepa, and I know that our side presented those ideas at the negotiations, but probably the military forces of the Zepa Brigade decided not to evacuate using that route. They probably did not feel safe and secure. I don't know what the reason was. I only know that after the population was evacuated, our forces were once again in a position to continue with the combat operations, and the combat operations continued. The Zepa Brigade was in retreat, moving in the direction of Zepske Kolibe and the trig point Zlovrh. Particularly fierce resistance was offered in that sector, Zlovrh and Zepske Kolibe. One of our commanders was wounded, Colonel Trivic, in the fighting at Zlovrh and Zepske Kolibe. And after two or three days of fighting, this area was also taken, and, indeed, I moved the communications centre of the forward command post to the Zlovrh hill where it remained for two or three days. That's where the forward command post of the Drina Corps was for that period. And then, on the basis of the intelligence that we received, we learned that the main force of the Zepa Brigade transferred to Serbia across the Drina River or, rather, at that time it was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So after the evacuation ended and before you moved the forward command post to Zlovrh in the intervening period, did you have an opportunity to hear General Mladic over the radio?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic was at the Glodjane forward command post after the evacuation ended, and he followed the operations conducted by our forces as they pursued the enemy towards Zepske Kolibe and Zlovrh. He had a pair of binoculars, and I think that he was talking to the commanders that were advancing along this axis. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when was the last time that you saw him in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe two days after the evacuation, approximately. That's when the pursuit operations in which enemy forces were pursued towards Zlovrh were conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And do you know where General Mladic went after that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, General Mladic left to the western theatre in Krajina by helicopter from a location nearby because news had been coming in about big problems that were going on at the western front in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at the very end, could I please have document P3038.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, could you please scroll down this document in the Serbian version so that we can see who signed it. That would be at page 2 of the English version. Mr. Jevdjevic, in the course of your evidence today you said several times -- or, rather, that during the day you knew about General Mladic's movements and that the last time that you saw him on the 11th of July was around 10 -- around 2200 hours at Bratunac Brigade. Here we have a document dated the 11th of July, 1995, that is signed by General Ratko Mladic, SR, and could you please tell us, in the heading of the document it is indicated Republika Srpska, strictly confidential number 03/41616. So in addition to what you knew, because you were a communications officer and this was your basic job in the army, could you tell us, where could this telegram have been sent from if you saw General Mladic in the Srebrenica and Bratunac area the whole day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic could use the equipment in the communications network to send this document to anyone from any communications centre that had encrypted teleprinter lines. Since I see on this stamp that is filled in by the cryptographers, this document was received at 1945 hours. It was encrypted by the cryptographer in two minutes. So it was processed at 1947, and then one minute later it was sent to the units. I assume that at that time, at the time when this document was drafted and signed, it should have already been drafted and signed, and I assume that General Mladic, given the time that he entered Srebrenica with General Krstic and General Zivanovic, he probably issued some other tasks and made the assessment of the situation that he couldn't have gone further than Bratunac. So I suppose he did have the technical capability to send it from the communications centre of the Bratunac Brigade because I saw him at 2200 hours when we had this meeting. The meeting ended at around 2300 hours. It is my opinion that this telegram -- well, he had the technical capabilities, and I assume that he sent it from the communications centre of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this completes my examination. There is a mistake in the transcript at page 2, I think, at line 2. Instead of cross-examination, it should read examination-in-chief, but that's not so important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you say, it isn't important. Mr. Zivanovic and Mr. Haynes, have you come to an agreement as to who is going first?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. We had a fortunate meeting in the street this afternoon, and I told Mr. Zivanovic I would go next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So take your time, Mr. Haynes, and go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to start by asking for the lectern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and if you could also kindly introduce yourself to the witness please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly. I was going to start by craving your indulgence, Mr. President. The examination of Mr. Petrusic has covered quite a lot of the areas which I had anticipated dealing with this witness, and accordingly I do not believe that the estimate I gave of, I think, four hours, is remotely accurate. I think it's more likely I'll be about half that time. But I would, notwithstanding the fact that we've had a shortened sitting today, welcome the opportunity of reviewing the transcript overnight before closing my examination in chief of this witness if that is okay with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, by how much shorter will your examination-in-chief --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If I was not clear - I thought I was - I thought -- it's about half as long as I anticipated it would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long -- so about two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have less than two hours. Let me just check the time now. According to the transcript, it's 1645. Yes. We have less than two hours, anyway, so that would not be a problem, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our suggestion is to have the break any time it's convenient to you between 5.30 and 5.40.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very kind of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You know who I am. I'm counsel for Vinko Pandurevic, and you and I had the opportunity to discuss the evidence you might give last week for a couple of days, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I really want to begin by giving the Court, through you, an overview of your professional relationship with Mr. Pandurevic during the course of the war in Bosnia. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to get to know Mr. Pandurevic before the war while he was serving in Slovenia. That was a brief acquaintance, and during the war I know that for a time, when he had just arrived in the army of Republika Srpska, he was the commander of the Visegrad Tactical Group, and after that the commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your capacity as commander of the Communications Battalion of the Drina Corps, you yourself took part in a number of operations in the field, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think on a number of occasions, you took part in operations that Vinko Pandurevic was also taking part in.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took part in several operations carried out in the area of the Drina Corps, and we participated together in some operations carried out in the zone of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm just going to run through them briefly, and I have authority, I think, to put the names and dates to you to save a bit of time. I think, firstly, in about March of 1993 you took part in an operation for Konjevic Polje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was an operation of the Drina Corps in which both I and Mr. Pandurevic as the commander of the Visegrad Brigade participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you just briefly describe for us what capacities each of you had in relation to that operation.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the communications battalion commander, and he was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the late spring and early summer of 1993, I think you took part in operations Mac 1 from Rogatica to Ustipraca and Mac 2 towards Gorazde and Cajnice. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I also participated in that operation as the commander of the communications battalion and the officer in charge of setting up the communications centre at the forward command post for that operation and Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, I think he was a major at the time, was then the commander of a combat group which participated in that operation Mac or Sword 1 on later on Mac or Sword 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to leave that there, but I want to come back to that in a little more detail later on. But I think in July of 1993, you also took part in Lukavac 93, an operation towards Trnovo, Bijelasnica, and Igman.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I participated in that operation, also, as an officer in charge of organising and setting up the communications centre for the unit from the Drina Corps which participated in the operations towards Igman and Bijelasnica. This operation was conducted in the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And for what it's worth, where was your forward command post in relation to that operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post -- my first forward command post was on Mount Jahorina at trig point 3009 metres, and later on in the town of Trnovo and later on in villages called Ledici, Ostojici and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. In the autumn of 1994, I think you took part in an operation in the Krajina in the area of Novi Grad where Vinko Pandurevic was your commander.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the needs of the combat in that part of the war theatre, the Drina Corps was given the task of establishing a brigade drawn from all the units and sending it to the western war theatre. The commander of that brigade was Major Pandurevic, and I was his deputy in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And that is another operation I'll come back to in a little more detail later on. But you've already told us that in the spring of 1995, you took part in Operation Spreca. Can you confirm that then-Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic was also a party to that operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic also participated in that operation. The 4th Serbian Brigade was introduced into the attack in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade so that his units were my right and left neighbours, and Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic was fully in command of his brigade during that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And your position within that operation was what?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that operation, I was the Chief of Staff of a temporary unit that was formed. It was in fact a brigade called the 4th Serbian Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more thing about Operation Spreca. Did that also involve, as an officer, Major Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Major Dragan Obrenovic also participated in that operation. He was the Chief of Staff in the Zvornik Brigade, and he was rather seriously wounded in the leg in the course of that operation due to an explosion of a mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
