utterances.text: Thank you. You've anticipated my next question. You've told us, and I won't say any more than this, about your involvement in Operations Krivaja 95 and Stupcanica 95. In August of 1995, were you also present at combat activities in Drvar in the Krajina where Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic was commander of a unit?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that period, the Drina Corps established a brigade from its composition and sent it to the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps, because there were huge problems in that period in that part of the battlefield. The commander of that brigade of the Drina Corps in that part of the war theatre was Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, and he remained there for a rather long period of time. I was in Drvar organising communications and carrying out an exchange of my men from the Communications Battalion, and I was at his forward command post for a few days, and then I returned to the corps command in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So if we can just summarise the state of your relationship, you knew Vinko Pandurevic as a soldier from his time in Slovenia I suppose until the time he left the army of Republika Srpska. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you knew him as a soldier both in peacetime and in wartime?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And to summarise what you've just told us in a few minutes, in the course of about 30 months you participated in eight combat operations with him. Take it from me, Mr. Jevdjevic, there are eight of them. Now, can we move on -- or, rather, backwards to Operations Mac 1 and Mac 2 in the spring of 1993. Who was responsible for the conduct of that operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Drina Corps, the commander of the forward command post was the then-operations officer of the Drina Corps, Colonel Dragomir Milosevic. He was a Colonel at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And your function?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task was to ensure communications -- or, rather, to set up the communications centre to be used to command that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in practical terms, what did that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practice, this meant that General -- or, rather, Colonel Milosevic at the time had to be provided with constant communications with all the combat groups participating in that operation. I should follow those communications and always be ready to intervene if they were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we'll deal with this in relation to three or four operations, but is the communications centre always synonymous with the forward command post of an operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications centre is only one of the elements of a forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But -- but in terms of geographical location, do they tend to be at the same place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all these operations, the communications centre is always in the same geographic location as the forward command post, and this may sound incredible but we all were within an area of some hundred square metres or so. These were small forward command posts, sometimes under a tent, often under a tent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we'll deal with this operation by operation as we go along, but I think we can all understand that you can hear communications between the commander and the units and possibly between the units on the ground. Did you tend as a communications officer to have visual capability as well? In other words, could you see what was going on in relation to these operations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was always duty-bound to follow the condition of the communications and the situation and to follow the conversations because that was the only way in which I could follow whether the communications were functioning, and in this way I understood the situation on the ground. But to organise communications in such cases, we always used radio equipment operating in a frequency range, which is such that the best quality communications are achieved if there is optical visibility, and all the commanders at the forward command post always try to be in a geographical location from which they could visually observe the battlefield and thus be in the best position to survey the situation in order to make the best possible decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer, but I sense you might just be talking a little bit too quickly for the translators, so just slow down a little bit. Now, I'm going to remind you now of Operations Mac 1 and Mac 2 by showing you a document, which is 65 ter 5D1169, an order of the 22nd of May. So could we have that into e-court, please. Do you have the document on your screen now, Mr. Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is a Main Staff document addressed to the commands of the Drina Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade. You can confirm that, can you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I just briefly would direct your attention to paragraph 2, and then I'd like the document, please, moved on so that you can see page 2 in the B/C/S, and we who speak English can see page 3, please. Let me know what you've finished reading.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's not a massive question, but does that recall for you the purposes of the operations you took part in in May and June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: As an aside, this operation, was it in a part of Bosnia that was very familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If nobody minds me leading, because your family came from there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in that part of Bosnia, and my family still lives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was it your understanding that the principal purpose of the operation to disarm Muslim formations and give civilians the choice of staying under Serbian rule or moving to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's in the document, but I'll move on. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to argue this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to argue. To quote Mr. McCloskey, we've got to finish this case sometime. Can we now move on, please, to 7D624 so that we can see, as it were, the effect of the operation on the ground. I'm hoping 65 ter 7D624 will come up in e-court soon. Now, I always feel like I'm taking my life in my hands by putting maps into e-court, but I think if we enlarge this twice and configure the screen so that Gorazde is in the bottom left-hand corner, Rogatica at the very top, and Visegrad on the far right. That's quite good. I think we might even be able to -- can Gorazde go down a little bit further? No, that's up. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to zoom further? It will make it more legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's try one zoom further because I'm going to attempt to get all the markings done on this in one go. Now, if we can push Visegrad over to the right, Rogatica up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have Gorazde --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, that's perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this is better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, that's as good as it gets. I think if at all possible, if Rogatica could just move a wee bit north, it would help, because we need the area beneath the river. That is perfect. Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We saw from the Main Staff order, Mr. Jevdjevic, that this was an operation which involved the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as well. In a short time, I'm going to ask you to be given a pen from which you can mark the screen, please, and I wonder if you could start by marking with an arrow the axis of the attack of the Sarajevo and Romanija Corps so far as you knew it.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume you are referring to the Drina Corps, because at that time we were carrying out operations in the general area of Gorazde, and that's what it says in the order sent from the Main Staff, which was the previous document. The front line and the task at the forward command post commanded by Colonel Milosevic, more or less from the positions then held by the Rogatica Brigade, Vrasalici, Cadovina, Trnovo, and Sljivno, the task was to come out on the left bank of the River Drina and disarm the Muslim militaries formations in that area and make it possible for the Muslim population either to move out of that area to other areas or to accept the political authority of the Republika Srpska. I remember that the forward command post to command that operation was first at an elevation near the village of Trnovo. Do I need to mark it with some letters?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. If you would put IKM1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as our forces advanced in the spirit of the task that they were assigned, we moved the forward command post to a hill here in the sector of the Lubardici, village, the village of Lubardici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You're thinking ahead of me. Now, the arrows that you've drawn on the map indicate which forces, Mr. Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that operation, there were two or three combat groups or battle groups that took part on the left bank of the River Drina, and there were the units from the Guards Brigade and from the Hercegovina Corps that took part in the operations in this area on the right bank of the Drina River. The objective of this operation in this area was to inflict a defeat on the Muslim formations deployed in this pocket from Ustipraca and to Medjedja and Brodari, where River Lim joins the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were any of those forces you've indicated under the command of then-Major Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Pandurevic commanded one of those formations, and I recall quite well that that formation included a battle group from his unit and some other battle groups from other units and his axis of attack in the spirit of the first arrow that I marked here, and that's this one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If you can make the letters small enough. I wonder if you could put a small VP by the side of that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've marked forward command post 1 and forward command post 2. Were there only two forward command posts during the course of this operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of this Operation Mac 1, I remember that we set up communications at the two forward command posts at the beginning of the operation in the village of Trnovo and for the second part of the operation here in the Lubardici sector. Later on, we moved in accordance with the tasks that we carried out to other sectors, Bogdanvici, Jandici and so on. And later on when the combat operations moved to the right bank of the Drina River as part of another operation, then the forward command post was in the Gradina sector near Cajnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. I'm really only concerned in this series of questions with the operation towards Ustipraca. How did the combat situation develop in that operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember from that period that the combat operations were done successively but that the decisive success was achieved by this formation under the command of Major Pandurevic, and after a while he and his unit and heavy artillery support pieces managed to get as far as the Drina River canyon overlooking Ustipraca. It's this place here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was the strategic significance of taking that position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When those groups from our forces reached those features, for all intents and purposes, all the units, all the enemy units remaining in the River Drina canyon from Ustipraca to Brodari were now in a very unfavourable position because this was the only route, the only valve, as we call it, that made it possible for them to pull out in the direction of Gorazde if the situation got unfavourable for them, and this was the military importance of it, reaching a strategic elevation that made it possible to control militarily the whole situation, because the artillery covered Ustipraca and the bridge at Ustipraca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meant that it was possible to fire on all military targets and all the other targets moving down that intersection and down the bridge towards Gorazde, and you could do that with direct fire, with line-of-sight fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder before I move on to the next few questions whether perhaps in blue or another colour you could indicate, as it were, where the enemy forces were situated.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I can only indicate with some accuracy the positions that the enemy forces held in this area in front of the forward command post. They held the high ground at Brcigovo, Sljedovici, Pokrivenik, and then further on to Dzankici and the intersection at Brodari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps it's my fault. I was inviting you to indicate where the forces of the enemy were located after the decisive action by Major Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this action was carried out, the enemy forces were pushed into the Drina River canyon approximately here. Those were the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at your communications centre, did you also have radio reconnaissance facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the communications centre at the forward command post, we had communications equipment that were used to exercise command in the course of this operation, and we had other equipment working at UKT range. Smaller battle groups among our forces had the same kind of equipment, so we used this radio equipment in order to have some control over the combat operations conducted at the front line itself to be able to hear what the smallest combat units deployed on their positions were doing, but we did not use this equipment to exercise command over those operations because we had equipment that made it possible to keep the data better protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll -- I'll go a different route. Did you become aware of any radio conversation between VRS forces and enemy forces during the course of this operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And who specifically were the correspondents in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point in the course of the operation, I heard over this radio that I told you about, I told you what the purpose was, I heard that the radio command network for the units commanded by Pandurevic was suddenly disrupted by a voice from the other side, and I heard Major Pandurevic engage this person in a military conversation. So to make myself clear, the forward command post of the corps under the command of Milosevic had equipment to exercise command over Pandurevic and other commanders, and Vinko Pandurevic in turn had different kind of equipment to exercise command over his subordinate units, and all of a sudden in this network an enemy soldier joined in. He obviously had been using that same frequency already, and he asked to be put in contact with Major Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it was a weird situation. That was the first time that something like that happened during the war, for two commanders from the opposing sides to engage in negotiations. And then I learned that this was Ahmet Sejdic, the commander of the Visegrad Brigade of the BH army which held that part of the front line, and he asked to talk to Major Pandurevic, and I personally listened in on that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you get the impression from what you heard that this was the first time they'd spoken to one another?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this was the first time that I heard this, I had an impression that they knew each other from before and that they had similar conversations over the radio before in the course of some previous combat operations in light of substantial familiarity that Ahmet Sejdic used when he addressed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did Ahmet Sejdic want?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Ahmet Sejdic literally asked him - because probably as he listened in, he learned that he was at the position that had fire control of the Ustipraca intersection and that held his unit, his troops, in their hands, so to speak - he asked Pandurevic to allow, to make it possible for an evacuation of the civilian population from this pocket to be carried out, the civilian population from Ustipraca and Medjedja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It may be that your answer's a little ambiguous. Who held whose units in their hands at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Units under the command of Vinko Pandurevic that reached the geographical point held the units of Ahmet Sejdic in their hands, to use non-military jargon. Ahmed Sejdic's units were in a very unfavourable position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was Pandurevic's response to this suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard Pandurevic say without much thought that he would agree with Ahmet Sejdic, saying that if Ahmet Sejdic thought it was a good thing to do that he would make sure that the civilian population from that area would withdraw to Gorazde and that Vinko Pandurevic and his units would make sure that not a single bullet would be fired from Vinko's positions during that evacuation. And then in the end, Vinko asked him, "How will I know that the entire column moved? Where would be the rear of the column? How will I be able to tell that all those who want to do so have withdrawn from that sector?" And I remember that Ahmet Sejdic told him, "I will be at the rear of the column driving a blue Mercedes." And this was really a striking thing, the thing that he mentioned, the blue Mercedes, in light of the fact that there was fierce fighting going on. So this was the conversation that I heard with my own ears, and this is what is actually done. And I know that Colonel Milosevic, the commander of the forward command post, did not interfere with this initiative of Major Pandurevic, but he automatically approved it. He didn't even get in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, was there one conversation between Pandurevic and Sejdic or more than one?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that conversation at that time, but talking over the radio that's not something that you just finish off by putting the receiver down, breaking off the connection. A radio communication can go on forever. It depends only on the wish of the participants to get on the line again and to perhaps deal with some details that need to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you've -- I think you've told us an evacuation did take place. How long after the conversation did the evacuation take place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume -- or, rather, I know that at that part of the front line there was a cease-fire and that the evacuation of the civilian population probably started. The information that we at the forward command post had was to the effect that those civilians moving in the column with vehicles, cars, other types of vehicles, also included a large number of members of the Muslim army because we did not encounter any substantial resistance in that area afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you see the evacuation yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to see the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you receive any information through the communications centre as to how many people left the area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not get the exact information as to how many people had left the area, but in that whole area there are just a few mountain villages and two large villages on the River Drina itself, Medjedja and Ustipraca, and I don't think that there were many people living there in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could you just complete your diagram for us then and show us in which direction the column evacuated from the area, in blue, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This column was moving from the direction of Brodari down that road along the Drina River, moved through Ustipraca, and then onwards to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you know how long it took?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know only that on that day, combat operations were suspended to allow the column to pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it -- I assume that this direction or this route that you have indicated is all the way along an existing road and not through woods or forests or whatever. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am quite familiar with the terrain there. As soon as the column passed through Ustipraca, it was probably moving in the area of the road, and that's where I drew it. That is the vicinity of the road. The last -- over the last 20 or 15 years, the road was on the left bank of the Drina River because of the hydroelectric plant. This map is an older one, and it shows a road on the right bank of the river, but I drew it in the vicinity of the road. This is where the road leading to Gorazde is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And that's where they wanted to go, to Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Sejdic told Vinko that this was the decision, the decision to go to Gorazde, and he asked him simply not to open fire from the dominant heights that he had taken and to allow them to travel down that road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Should we have the break now, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I could just finish this topic with about three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course. Yes, but I don't know that he is finished with this document. If he has, then we'll ask him to sign now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I don't require any further markings on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you please put on the document, Mr. Jevdjevic, your initials and today's date, which is the 11th of December of 2008.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can that be preserved, please? Yes, done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just a couple more things. When the forces of the army of Republika Srpska entered what I will call the pocket, did they find any remaining Muslim army units there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that later on, the combat operations were directed elsewhere in the direction of Medjedja and Dzankici but that in this operation this pocket from Ustipraca to Brodari was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps the question wasn't clear enough. Did it appear that all army units that had been there, all Muslim army units, had, as it were, walked out with the column or driven out?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Haynes. Twenty minutes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to ask you three or four more questions about Ustipraca in 1993, and then we'll move on. At the time of the movement of the column, were you aware of any instruction to attempt to disarm any members of that column before it was allowed through to Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That column was allowed through to Gorazde without any fire being opened on it at the cost of having armed Muslim soldiers pull out under cover of that convoy, but the command didn't want to risk opening fire even though they assumed there were soldiers among the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And secondly, before reaching an agreement with Ahmet Sejdic, did Vinko Pandurevic seek any approval from his superior command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a decision he made on his own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did his actions surprise you, Mr. Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the first time in the course of the war that I heard two commanders of opposing sides negotiating on very important issues, because at that time everyone was very exclusive, and I was surprised that Major Pandurevic, without consulting his superior command, made the decision to allow the column through, and he allowed them to pass before the barrels of his guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll leave that topic there. I just want to briefly move forward to the Krajina in the autumn of 1994 where you've told us that Vinko Pandurevic was a commander of a Tactical Unit and you were his deputy. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that was operations in the area of Novi Grad. During the course of those operations, did your unit suffer any particular logistical problems?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that in the initial stage of carrying out those combat activities, we crossed the road leading from Novi Grad toward Buzim in a canyon and that with a swift action we pushed back the enemy forces from their trenches and practically adhered to them on the hill on the other side of the canyon. The forward command post where Pandurevic was remained on the first side of the canyon, as did all our logistics, so that it was very difficult for us to supply the units adhering to the enemy on the opposite side of the canyon. It was hard to supply them with ammunition, food, and water.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were the difficulties with ammunition in relation to the unit you commanded?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was on that other side of the canyon with the units that had got stuck to the enemy side at a distance of some 100 to 200 metres. We held those positions, and the unit I was with in front was experiencing problems in supplies of ammunition, because every day we suffered fierce counter-attacks from the enemy side, which was attempting to push us out of their trenches, which we had taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What means did Major Pandurevic use to supply you with ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only way for us to be replenished with ammunition because of the completely impassable terrain was for that ammunition to be carried to us on foot, and the only bearers who could be used on that terrain were people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you tell us what people were used?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that part of the front line, as it was in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, the original command assigned to us several men who were fulfilling a work obligation. They were not military conscripts. They had a work obligation, and these men were assigned to carry the supplies of ammunition and other supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who is Miladin Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miladin Pandurevic was a soldier of mine, a communications man who for the needs of organising communications in that temporary unit, that brigade commanded by Pandurevic had the task of implementing communications. He is a close relative, a cousin, to Colonel Pandurevic, who is now a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did he take part in the running of ammunition to your trenches?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well on one occasion when the group carrying ammunition arrived, since it was something that was badly needed, seeing Miladin Pandurevic in the group. He's older than me, and when I saw the commander, Milenko Jovanovic, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade Staff Command, he was the commander of the headquarters of that brigade commanded by Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to clear that up, what role was Milenko Jovanovic playing in all this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the headquarters administration in the Zvornik Brigade, and when the brigade was formed for activities in the area of the 1st Krajina Corps, he was the commander of the headquarters administration of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But in relation to the running of ammunitions. Was he doing anything in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His general duty was to look after supplies for the headquarters or the command of the brigade where Pandurevic and I were, but Pandurevic engaged him, Milenko Jovanovic and Miladin Pandurevic who were supposed to carry the ammunition together with the people who had a work obligation and who were assigned to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the people who had the work obligation, were they Serbs, Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they arrived on the other side, this whole group, when they came to where I was, I learned that they had a work obligation, that they resided near Novi Grad, and that they were all Muslims, and I found it very unusual in that combat situation that General Pandurevic, as we needed more ammunition and didn't have enough men, in fact sent his brother and his headquarters administration commander or commander of the staff command together with those men, for all of them to bring that ammunition to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to move forward now to Krivaja 95, and I'm going to try as best I can not to ask you the same questions that Mr. Petrusic has asked you. How long before you established the communications centre at Pribicevac did you first know about Operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was most probably the chief of communications of the Drina Corps who informed me of that task a day or two before I left, that is, on the 3rd or 4th of July, and he handed me the documents concerning communications for the implementation of that operation. I assume it might have been the 4th of July, the day before I left for the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is that a usual period of time to be given to prepare a communications centre for a combat operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In wartime, we were all used to acting ad hoc. When a task was assigned, we would accept it. There was no precise time limit. But as far as I was concerned, it was quite sufficient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I want to return previously to a document you've looked at before, and that is P3753. I apologise that on my list of documents I've used P3893, which is precisely similar, but P3753 is the better version of that document. Just a few little details about this that I don't think you've been asked. Did you write that document, or did somebody else do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was drawn up by the chief of communications of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think I can probably lead you on this. His name's Nedo Blagojevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to clear up a couple of things about the document itself. If we go across to column number 4 and column number 5, we see there 22 numbers with frequencies written after them -- written after them. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the main frequency, is that number 1?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the frequency we started combat operations with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You say started. You were in the communications centre throughout the period from the 5th of July until the 11th. Were you ever aware that any of the other 21 reserved frequencies was used at all?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As we had secure equipment and that frequency behaved very well in maintaining communications by day and by night, there was no need to change it. So we used it all the way up to the end of the Operation Krivaja, and I assume it was even used in the Stupcanica 95 operation, also, because we were absolutely sure that the lines were secure, the ones that these two operations were carried out with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to go back to column number 1, and if we go - one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight - nine rows down, we'll see -- we see there's a provision there for MUP with the code-name Oblak. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: During the whole period from the 5th to the 11th of July, was there ever a MUP unit who was using the network for Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We know that at some stage a Special Police unit was present in -- in the area of Srebrenica and its environ. Was there a discussion about whether they should be joined to any network that was operated by you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make everything clear, when I received this communications plan, which was probably on the 4th of July, as I said, I looked at who all the participants were who were due to take part in the operation. As it was very important for me that if one of those units did not have secure equipment, I should provide them from my reserves in the Communications Battalion. Sometimes, such situations did occur. And then I noticed that MUP was a participant, so I asked either Nedo Blagojevic or General Krstic, because I know that MUP units did not have this equipment which provided a secure line that the army had, so I asked what sort of unit this was and whether I should provide them with equipment. What I recall from that period of time is that MUP, which was included in the plan, would not participate in the offensive action against Srebrenica, in the assault, and what I remember is that this probably referred to the members of the local police stations who were subordinate to the Zvornik public security centre. I apologise for such a lengthy reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. Was it your understanding that, as it were, MUP units generally had access to the sort of secure communications devices that you were using within this network?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of Operation Krivaja 95, the MUP units did not appear in the radio network. So I assume that they did not have the equipment of this kind because only the army had this equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before we leave this document, one other, as it were, unit I want to ask you about. Are you familiar with the 10th Sabotage Detachment Unit?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's obvious from the document that they don't appear to be a unit that you were advised would be part of your network in this operation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is there any serious contest to that question? I mean, read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I stand by my objection. I can explain it if we want to, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if the witness understands English or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's probably easier if I move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Had you been informed that that unit would take part in Operation Krivaja 95 prior to the commencement of combat?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you become aware of their presence in the area around Srebrenica at some time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They appeared in the combat zone. I think it was on the 10th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you remember whether that was before, after, or at about the same time that you first saw General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic also came to the forward command post on the 10th of July, and this unit showed up at that part of the front line near Pribicevac on the 10th of July, but I don't know the specifics. I assume that they arrived a bit later than General Mladic because he arrived at around 0900 hours, so that I'm almost certain that they came to that sector after him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did they have a signalsman in their unit?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I learned that this unit appeared in the combat zone, I knew that they did not have the equipment with the scrambler devise that we had in the course of this operation, and I simply asked General Krstic in an effort to find a solution, asking him when I would be asked to provide them with such equipment and what activities they would be involved in in order to be able to exercise command over them. And this is where I actually met their signalsman and we discussed this problem, because signalsmen are those who have to deal with the problem of establishing communications. He told me that they had those small ultra shortwave equipment, Motorolas, as they were called, and that these were quite sufficient for them and that he did not intend to carry this large piece of equipment around with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you remember what his name was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His last name was Bobar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you learn from him any of the details of his assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that they had some special assignment. I didn't pay much attention to it because General Mladic was there and so was General Krstic. I think that they had maybe 20 or 30 men there. It was a small unit, and its name speaks to its purpose. It was a specialised unit, specialised to carry out certain tasks, specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in terms of the communications centre at Pribicevac, were -- was there, as it were, more than one facility at Pribicevac to deal with the command of the units? That's probably a bad question, but was there an observation post as well as the forward command post itself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an observation post at Kula, a few hundred metres away from the location of the forward command post itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was there visual capability from the forward command post so that you could see, as it were, the combat activities going on?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this equipment was portable, it was enough for us to move some 20 metres and to be able to see the slopes of Zeleni Jadar on the other side and to see all the key features in the combat zone and, for the most part, the road leading from Zeleni Jadar to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And in terms of the observation post, what was it you could see from there that you couldn't see from the forward command post proper?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the observation post, you could see the town of Srebrenica, all of it, I think, and the valley leading from Srebrenica to Potocari. And it was possible to see the entire area much better than you could from the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever go to the observation post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of Operation Krivaja 95, I did not go to the observation post where General Mladic was, but before this operation was launched I went to the observation post several times, and you have the whole area in sight from there. I didn't really need to go there because I was able to follow the combat operations from the small observation post located at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But these are really foundational questions. Did you talk to people who'd been up to the observation post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we've got seven or eight minutes, and I'm going to try and achieve something in that time. I want you to help us with how the communications worked during Operation Krivaja 95. Firstly, I want to deal with communications from the IKM to the units on the ground, which is the document we've just been looking at, as I understand it. What was the system that was used to communicate with the units on the ground from the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that a question? Am I supposed to answer it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. What was the system which you used to communicate, for example, with Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all the units that participated in Operation Krivaja 95 and that are contained in this communications plan that we see on the screen, we had the RUP-2/2K equipment that had a scrambler devise. That was called KZU 63. That is the encryption protection device 63. That's what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as far as you are aware, were communications on that network capable of interception?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the knowledge that I have both from that period and the knowledge that I obtained since, in all combat operations, not only Krivaja and Stupcanica 95 but in all other operations, the conversations that were protected using this device were never intercepted. It was not possible to carry out audio surveillance of those conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question about that network. Was that an open network so that whenever anybody spoke on it, everybody else who was on the network could hear?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an open network where all the participants -- whenever a participant is talking, all the other participants hear him. When he presses the button of the micro-telephonic communication, all the participants in the network can hear him, and when he releases the button, then his transmitter is switched off, and then other participants can talk. So it was an open network. We had aerials with radial electromagnetic wave transmission in all directions. In other words, it was very flexible and reliable, and it made it possible to exercise command in those operations, and it was fully protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move on to the communications between the forward command post and corps command and the Main Staff. By what equipment was that set up?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the forward command post, in addition to this -- the communications that were used with the subordinate units, I had to establish communications with the superior command, the Drina Corps Command at Vlasenica. The communications were established using a radio relay device RRU1 in a radio relay section up to the Veliki Zep node, and from there the communications joined in the standard system of radio relay communications leading to Vlasenica. Using encrypted teleprinters, we could receive and transmit written documents that were protected, encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how would you establish voice communication with, for example, the corps command at Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the forward command post in Pribicevac, using the radio relay device 1, RRU1 that I spoke about, we were able to get a three-digit number which was, in effect, an extension of the telephone exchange that was located at the Main Staff, and this same number but with different digits was at the Drina Corps command at their exchange. The exchanges are used to transmit calls further on or to put two participants in radio communication in contact. If I wanted to call the Drina Corps command in Vlasenica from the Pribicevac forward command post, all I needed to do was to dial 332, and then I would get the operator at the exchange, at the switchboard in the corps command, and then I was able through him to talk to all the other participants in the Drina Corps area and all the other participants and users of telephone communications in Bosnia and Herzegovina and further afield.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was -- was that a protected line, or was that an open line?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an open line if we're talking about voice communications, whereas written documents were protected using encryption devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you for today, Mr. Jevdjevic, and it's just been pointed out to me it's your birthday. Happy birthday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I have an indication from you, Mr. Haynes, how much longer do you think you will --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think maybe an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And you, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: About half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And you, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I better stick with my original, but I hope -- I hope it's much shorter. My original was five, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want the witness, first of all, to -- and Mr. Bourgon, yes? Two hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One hour, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. So more or less, that's it. You're going to be with us tomorrow and definitely a good part of next week. We stand -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we actually put down that we have approximately 30 to 45 minutes, but -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but I was concentrating on the main ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we're talking about a few days next week as well. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 12th day of December, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
